questions.prompt: What does 'shift left' mean in the secure SDLC?

options.text: Move security earlier in development, where flaws are cheaper to fix
Move security to the very end, just before release

questions.explanation: Shifting left moves security activities earlier (design and coding), catching flaws when they cost a fraction of production fixes.

questions.prompt: Match each security-testing tool to what it inspects.

pairs.right: A running application from the outside

questions.explanation: SAST reads code, DAST attacks the running app, SCA checks dependencies, and secret scanning catches committed credentials — layered, they cover different flaws.

questions.prompt: A machine-readable inventory of every component in your software is called an ____ (acronym).
questions.explanation: An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) lets you instantly tell which systems are affected when a new dependency vulnerability is disclosed.

questions.prompt: Which defend the software supply chain (OWASP A08)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Signing artifacts and using build provenance (SLSA)

questions.explanation: Dependency management, SBOMs, and signed/provenance-tracked builds defend the supply chain; blindly trusting dependencies is the risk.

items.text: On pull request: SAST, SCA, secret and IaC scans
On build: generate an SBOM and sign the image
On deploy to test: DAST against the running app

questions.explanation: Static and dependency checks run at pull-request time, SBOM/signing at build, and dynamic testing against a running app after deploy to a test env.

questions.prompt: Why can security tooling that's too slow or noisy end up protecting nothing?

options.text: Teams get exemptions and bypass it, so it must be fast and tuned to be followed
Slow tools find more real bugs

questions.explanation: Security that blocks delivery or floods developers with false positives gets routed around; guardrails must be fast and trustworthy to actually be used.
